reference.source: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology / Oxford Textbook of Medicine
clinicalPearls: An inherited disorder of dibasic amino acid transport in the proximal tubule and gut, causing recurrent cystine stones from childhood or early adulthood
Suspect it in any young patient with recurrent radio-opaque stones, a family history, or bilateral or staghorn calculi
Cystine is the only one of the four affected amino acids (cystine, ornithine, lysine, arginine) that is poorly soluble and forms stones
The urine sediment classically shows flat hexagonal cystine crystals, which are essentially pathognomonic
A positive urinary cyanide-nitroprusside screening test supports the diagnosis, confirmed by quantitative urinary cystine excretion

Cornerstones of prevention are high fluid intake to dilute the urine, urinary alkalinisation (for example with potassium citrate) since cystine is more soluble at higher pH, and dietary sodium restriction
Thiol-binding agents that increase cystine solubility are reserved for stones refractory to fluid and alkalinisation measures
reference.pathophysiology: Cystinuria results from defective transport of the dibasic amino acids cystine, ornithine, lysine and arginine across the apical membrane of proximal renal tubular cells and intestinal epithelium. Biallelic mutations in SLC3A1 (encoding the rBAT subunit) or SLC7A9 (encoding the b0,+AT subunit) impair reabsorption, so large amounts of cystine reach the urine. Because cystine is relatively insoluble at normal urinary pH, it precipitates and aggregates into recurrent calculi, with solubility improving as pH rises. Stone burden and obstruction can produce recurrent colic, infection and, over time, chronic kidney damage.
additionalDifferentials: Calcium oxalate or calcium phosphate nephrolithiasis
Distal renal tubular acidosis with nephrocalcinosis
additionalInvestigations: Urine microscopy for characteristic hexagonal cystine crystals
24-hour urinary cystine quantification and supersaturation assessment
Stone composition analysis by infrared spectroscopy or X-ray crystallography
Non-contrast CT or ultrasound to define stone burden and hydronephrosis
Genetic testing of SLC3A1 and SLC7A9 where confirmation or counselling is needed
redFlags: Obstructing stone with fever or sepsis requiring urgent decompression
Bilateral or staghorn calculi threatening renal function
Progressive decline in glomerular filtration from recurrent obstruction
Anuria or acute kidney injury from bilateral obstruction or a solitary kidney
reference.prognosis: With lifelong high fluid intake, urinary alkalinisation and monitoring, stone recurrence can be markedly reduced, but adherence is demanding and recurrent stones or interventions may lead to chronic kidney disease over decades.
pitfalls: Attributing recurrent stones to idiopathic calcium disease and missing the cystine diagnosis on crystal morphology
Under-dosing fluid intake so urine remains supersaturated overnight when stones typically form
Neglecting dietary sodium reduction, which independently increases urinary cystine excretion
Assuming a negative nitroprusside screen fully excludes the disorder without quantitative cystine measurement
